parsed.summary: The file states four NP-hardness results under deterministic polynomial-time Karp reductions from every NP language (TM2 polytime model, bit-string encodings): (1) GapCVP in ℓ2 with gap n^{1/400}, for nonsingular integer bases and integer targets; (2) binary nearest codeword with gap n^{1/200}; (3) binary syndrome decoding with gap n^{1/200}; (4) GapCVP in ℓp for each rational p ≥ 1 with gap n^{1/(200p)}. Items (1)–(3) match Theorem 1 and Corollary 15 of the excerpt. The most important caveat is that the ℓp statement (4) and its gap exponent are not in the excerpt, and it drops the integer-target requirement, so it cannot be checked against the paper. The `disjoint` fields are sorry'd but appear true.

glossary.plain: L ∈ NP: there exist a polynomial bound and a polytime TM2 verifier V such that L(x) ⇔ ∃ certificate c with |c| ≤ bound(|x|) and V(x,c) = true.
A polytime map f with x ∈ L ⇒ f(x) ∈ YES and x ∉ L ⇒ f(x) ∈ NO.
glossary.standard_concept: Karp reduction to a promise problem

glossary.plain: Every NP language Karp-reduces to the promise problem.
Self-delimiting (length-prefixed) concatenation of dimension, radius, target and basis rows.
glossary.standard_concept: binary encoding of a CVP instance
glossary.note: Injective because the dimension comes first and every field is length-prefixed.

glossary.plain: det B ≠ 0 and r > 0. The conjunct 0 ≤ n is vacuous; n = 0 is allowed since the det of the empty matrix is 1.
glossary.note: n = 0 instances are degenerate but harmless.

glossary.standard_concept: squared Euclidean distance to the lattice point Bv

glossary.plain: YES: an encoded instance with integer t, well-formed, and dist₂(t, L(B)) ≤ r. NO: an encoded instance with integer t, well-formed, and every v satisfies dist > n^{1/400}·r.
glossary.note: Comparing squares is equivalent to comparing distances since r > 0.

glossary.plain: YES: n > 0, R > 0, and ∃ c with wt(u − Gc) ≤ R. NO: n > 0, R > 0, and ∀ c, wt(u − Gc) > n^{1/200}·R.
YES: ∃ x with Hx = b and wt(x) ≤ R. NO: the system Hx = b is consistent, and every solution x has wt(x) > n^{1/200}·R.
glossary.note: NO additionally requires consistency, matching the proof sketch.

glossary.plain: ℓp GapCVP with gap n^{1/(200p)}, rational p ≥ 1, rational target allowed.
glossary.note: The ℓp statement is not in the excerpt.

lean_claims.plain: Every NP language Karp-reduces in polytime to GapCVP_{n^{1/400}} (ℓ2, integer target, nonsingular integer basis).
Every NP language reduces to binary nearest codeword with gap n^{1/200}.
Every NP language reduces to binary syndrome decoding with gap n^{1/200}.
For each rational p ≥ 1, every NP language reduces to ℓp GapCVP with gap n^{1/(200p)}.

paper_claims.plain: GapCVP_{n^{1/400}} is NP-hard under deterministic polytime many-one reductions (nonsingular B ∈ Z^{n×n}, t ∈ Z^n, r ∈ Q_{>0}).
Binary nearest codeword and binary syndrome decoding are NP-hard to approximate within n^{1/200}.

flags.explanation: The ℓp result (gap n^{1/(200p)}, p rational ≥ 1) is not in the excerpt, so the exponent and the range of p cannot be checked. Unlike gapCVP400, this promise omits hasIntegerTarget, so the YES/NO sets admit rational targets. Larger target sets make a reduction easier, so this is slightly weaker than an integer-target version.
flags.probe_idea: Compare with the paper's ℓp corollary; optionally add hasIntegerTarget to the YES and NO conditions.

flags.explanation: The disjointness fields of all four promises are `sorry`. If one were false, the promise would be ill-formed. They appear true: encodings are injective, the gap factor is ≥ 1 when n ≥ 1, and the n = 0 cases give 0^x = 0, which makes NO false.
flags.probe_idea: Prove each disjoint field, e.g. ∀ bits, yesLanguage bits → noLanguage bits → False, using injectivity of encodeInstance.

flags.explanation: Dimension 0 is allowed (det of the empty matrix = 1), and the conjunct 0 ≤ dimension is vacuous. Such instances can only be YES, so this is harmless.
NO requires Hx = b to be solvable. This shrinks the NO set, making the Lean statement slightly stronger, and it matches the paper's proof setup.
